title: Files, Documents, Images, and Search: How Applications Find Information
description: Not everything a product knows fits into rows and columns. Learn where files actually live, how a database record points at a file it cannot hold, and how an application chooses between filtering, keyword search, and semantic search to deliver the right information to an AI.

objectives.label: Distinguish structured, semi-structured, and unstructured information and why each changes the architecture
Explain how a database record about a file relates to the file itself in object storage
Match a retrieval question to the right tool: database filter, keyword search, or semantic search
Trace the pipeline that turns an uploaded document into information an AI can answer from

lessons.title: When facts stop fitting in tables

slides.title: The report does not fit in a row

blocks.text:
A nonprofit tracker stores each organization's name, city, category, and whether it is active. Those facts fit a table, and a database can filter them. The same organization also has a 40-page annual report, photos, flyers, and meeting recordings. There is no honest column called annual_report_paragraph_1.

A database can technically store a large file inside a row. That does not mean it should. The database is built to query named facts, keep relationships, and check permissions. File storage is built to hold the bytes. A search system is built to find a passage inside those files. Good architecture gives each part the job it is good at. The question has changed from how to organize facts to how to organize knowledge that does not arrive as fields.

A computer that stores the PDF has the file. It does not automatically understand the paragraphs, tables, and photos the way a person does. Having access to a file is not the same thing as understanding its contents.

blocks.alt: Three kinds of information: a structured student record with named fields, a semi-structured JSON document whose fields can vary, and an unstructured PDF full of paragraphs and photos
blocks.caption: The system knows the shape of the first, half-knows the second, and receives the third as a file.
steps: Structured: student_id, name, county, graduation_year — the system knows exactly what each value means
Semi-structured: a JSON document whose fields can differ from record to record, like API payloads and logs
Unstructured: a PDF full of paragraphs, tables, photos and charts — it arrives as one file

blocks.text:
Structured information already has a shape the system understands. A student row with student_id 7281, name Maya, county Tulsa, and graduation_year 2027 can answer who is in Tulsa County, because each value has a name. Databases are powerful here: the question maps onto fields that already exist.

Semi-structured information is organized, but the shape can change from one record to the next. A JSON payload might list Tulsa Youth Sports, an array of programs, and a contact email nested inside. API responses and logs often look like this. You can read the fields that showed up. You cannot assume every record has the same columns a single table would require.

Unstructured information arrives as one file, such as a community impact report PDF. Paragraphs, tables, photos, names, and statistics may all be inside it. Until something extracts them, the application cannot filter a county out of that file the way it filters a column. The system knows the student row, half-knows the JSON, and receives the report as a file.

blocks.question: A scanned grant application arrives as one PDF. Which form of information is it?

options.label: Structured, because the application received it as a file
Unstructured, because the system receives one file and does not automatically understand the paragraphs inside
Semi-structured, because PDFs travel through APIs like JSON
Structured, because the document contains names and dates

blocks.explanation: The system receives the PDF as a file. Names and dates exist inside it, but the application cannot address them as fields the way it can address a student's county. Until something extracts structure, the document is unstructured information.

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: Having access to a file is not the same thing as understanding its contents.

blocks.alt: An application connected to three systems: a database holding structured facts, file storage holding the actual files, and a search index holding structures built for finding information
blocks.caption: These systems are not competing with each other. Each is optimized for a different kind of work, and a real product may use all three at once.
steps: Database: organization IDs, names, categories, permissions — facts the system can query
File storage: the actual PDFs, photos, videos and recordings
Search index: prepared structures that make information findable

blocks.text:
The three systems are specialists. The database holds facts it can query: ids, names, categories, and who is allowed to see a record. Object storage holds the bytes of the PDF, the photo, or the recording. A search index holds structures prepared ahead of time so a question can find a passage without opening every file.

On a laptop demo, a file can sit in a folder on that one disk. A product people share cannot treat each upload as another ordinary column, and it cannot assume the folder is still there after the machine restarts. Object storage gives the file an id or a location and holds the object. Services such as Amazon S3 or Azure Blob Storage do this job. You do not need their APIs to use the split.

The database helps the application know what the object is. Object storage holds the object itself. A real product often needs all three: the row, the file, and the index that makes the file findable.

blocks.title: Maya uploads a report
steps: Maya uploads tulsa-youth-sports-annual-report-2026.pdf. One click has to update two systems that do different jobs.
The PDF bytes go to object storage at a location such as /files/organizations/381/reports/2026-report.pdf. That address points at the object. It is not a column full of paragraphs.
The database creates a document row: document_id 9127, organization_id 381, the filename, document_type annual_report, and the upload time. Those fields say what the file is and who it belongs to.
The same row stores storage_location, aimed at the object outside the database. The organization points at the document row. The document row points at the file. One link leaves the database.
Permissions stay on the row, so the app can refuse someone who does not belong to organization 381. The bytes stay in storage. The record is the relationship that crosses the two systems.

blocks.question: A user opens a document page and sees the PDF. What did the database contribute to that moment?

options.label: The PDF bytes themselves, stored in a documents table
The document's ID, owner, type and the location of the actual file in storage
A copy of every paragraph, for fast reading
Nothing — the file storage does all the work

blocks.explanation: The database stores facts about the file: who it belongs to, what type it is, and where the bytes live. The record is a relationship that crosses systems, pointing outside the database to the object that holds the file itself.

slides.title: What it is, versus the thing itself

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: The database helps the application know what the object is. Object storage holds the object itself.

blocks.alt: Three questions mapped to three retrieval tools: show active organizations in Tulsa goes to a database filter, find documents containing basketball goes to text search, and find programs for a teenager who enjoys sports goes to semantic search
blocks.caption: Different retrieval problems require different tools. Fast retrieval also requires preparation: an index is work done before the search so the search can be quick.
steps: "Show active organizations in Tulsa" → database filter: records whose fields match conditions
"Find documents containing basketball" → keyword search: scan the text of documents
"Find programs for a teenager who enjoys sports" → semantic search: match by meaning, not exact words
Pipelines combine them: filter by county and status first, then semantic-search within that smaller set

blocks.text:
Show active organizations in Tulsa is a database filter. The rows already have county, category, and active, so the engine returns the ones whose fields match. It is precise, and it is fast when those fields are indexed. It cannot invent a field. If the annual report says Saturday programs run basketball leagues, and nobody stored offers_basketball as true, the filter will not find that sentence.

Find documents containing basketball is keyword search over the text. It can hit basketball league or basketball coaching. It misses a document that says youth athletics, or athletic opportunities for adolescents, because the letters differ even when a person would call the ideas the same.

Find programs for a teenager who enjoys sports needs similarity of meaning. A real product often chains the tools: filter to Tulsa and active first, then search by meaning inside that smaller set, then rank the matches. Searching the entire collection for every question is the slow version of the same pipeline.

slides.title: When the words do not match

blocks.text:
A user searches for opportunities for teenagers who enjoy sports. A fitting page says the group organizes basketball leagues for students ages 14 to 18. Almost none of the words are shared. A person still sees the match. A keyword index does not, because it is comparing letters.

An embedding turns a piece of text into a mathematical representation of its meaning, so the computer can compare pieces by how close those representations sit. Basketball for teenagers and youth sports program land near each other. A page of tax instructions lands somewhere else. Searching on those representations is semantic search, also called vector search.

The embedding does not replace a filter for an exact fact. County and active status are still columns with exact values. Semantic search is for the question those columns were never built to answer.

blocks.question: The product needs to find organizations in Oklahoma County that are currently active. Which retrieval tool fits?

options.label: Semantic search, because county and status are complicated ideas
Keyword search over every stored document
A database filter on the county and active fields
Ask the AI model to read every organization record

blocks.explanation: The question is about named fields with exact values, which is what a database filter is built for: precise, fast and predictable. Keyword and semantic search solve different problems — matching words inside documents and matching meaning — and would be slower and less precise here.

slides.title: Upload a PDF, ask a question

blocks.alt: A pipeline from an uploaded PDF through file storage, a document record, text extraction, chunking and indexing into a search system; later a user question triggers search and retrieval and the retrieved passages go to the AI, which generates an answer
blocks.caption: Find first, generate second — that order is the whole idea behind retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG.
steps: User uploads a PDF → file storage keeps the original
Database creates the document record
Text extraction reads the text out of the PDF
Chunking breaks the document into useful sections
Indexing prepares the sections for search
Later: a question triggers search and retrieval of the strongest passages
The AI receives the question plus the retrieved passages and generates the answer

blocks.text:
Upload a PDF and ask questions sounds like one feature. It is a pipeline. The original file goes to object storage, a document row is created, extraction reads words out of the PDF, chunking breaks a long report into sections, and indexing prepares those sections. Later a question searches, retrieves a few strong passages, and hands the question plus those passages to the model.

You do not hand the model every document. Twenty PDFs might fit in one prompt. Two million will not. Extra pages also add cost, delay, and irrelevant text the model may treat as the answer. The useful shape is a large collection, then search, then a small subset, then the model. Find first, generate second. That order is retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG.

Chunking is how page 187 can be the thing you retrieve. A 300-page report is a poor single object to search. The system can return the section that says the summer program served 438 students, instead of the whole book. Too large a chunk buries the answer. Too small a chunk cuts the answer off from the sentence that makes it true. A wrong answer is often born before the model: weak extraction, a bad chunk, a missing index, or retrieval that returned the wrong pages. Editing the prompt does nothing if the right page never arrived.

blocks.question: The PDF answers the user's question on page 187, but the AI answers wrongly and the prompt looks fine. What is a likely cause?

options.label: The AI model forgot how to read
The page was never extracted, was chunked badly, or retrieval returned the wrong sections
The database stored the PDF incorrectly
The user asked in the wrong language

blocks.explanation: A bad answer can be born long before the model: weak extraction, poor chunking, bad indexing or bad retrieval all deliver the wrong information to a perfectly fine model. Changing the prompt at the bottom of that pipeline may accomplish nothing.

slides.title: The right information at the right moment

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: An AI model does not need to know everything. The surrounding system needs to deliver the right information at the right moment.

slides.title: The catalog is built before the question

blocks.text:
A library with a million books can answer "do you have a book by Andy Weir?" by walking every shelf and opening every book. That works, and it is a bad design. An index is a structure prepared ahead of the question: a catalog for authors, a database index on county or email, a text index for the word basketball, a vector index for nearby meanings.

Without that preparation, storing the files was cheap and every search is slow. With it, you spend computation and storage up front so the later question can jump. At 20 documents you will not feel the difference. At 20 million, the search that opens everything stops being a product.

The index is also a copy of a decision you already made. If the report changes and nobody rebuilds the chunks and the index, search keeps returning the old passage. Fast retrieval is work done before the question, and that work has to be redone when the source changes.

slides.title: A photo does not contain the word

blocks.text:
photo_128783.jpg is the image object. The file does not contain a searchable sentence that says what is in the picture. What the product can filter lives beside it as structured metadata: who uploaded it, when, where, the caption, the tags, the width, and the height.

A vision model can add another layer. It might describe the file as teenagers playing basketball in an indoor gym, and list basketball, people, and gym. That description is text the search index can use. The image stays an image in object storage. The new words are derived information, not pixels.

The same transformation shows up everywhere a file is opaque. Audio becomes a transcript. A PDF becomes extracted text and tables. A photo becomes a description. Products often turn unstructured information into something structured or searchable, and that preparation is part of the architecture, not a flourish after the upload.
